about: Every figure the docs quote from a study, survey, vendor or regulator: the value, what it measures, where it comes from, when it was last checked, and the source's own words. tests/test_evidence.py keeps the docs and this file in step. Re-check an entry at its URL before changing its figure.

entries.claim: the size of the planted-failure test page
entries.source: UK Government Digital Service, What we found when we tested tools on the world's least-accessible webpage (2017-02-24)
entries.quote: At the moment it contains a total of 143 failures grouped into 19 categories.

entries.claim: the share of the planted barriers found by the best single tool: 37% counting errors and warnings (Tenon), 41% counting manual-inspection prompts (Asqatasun)
entries.source: UK Government Digital Service (2017-02-24)
entries.quote: If we only count error messages and warnings, then Tenon picked up the most barriers – it found 37% of them. If we also count manual inspection prompts, then Asqatasun was the most effective – it found 41% of the barriers.

entries.claim: the share of the planted barriers found by the ten tools combined
entries.source: UK Government Digital Service (2017-02-24)
entries.quote: While the tools picked up the majority of the accessibility barriers we created – 71% – there was a large minority that would only have been picked up by manual checking.

entries.claim: the share of the planted barriers found by no tool
entries.source: UK Government Digital Service (2017-02-24)
entries.quote: We found that a large proportion of the barriers we created weren't picked up by any of the 10 tools we tested – 29% in fact.

entries.claim: the share of accessibility issues, by volume, that fully automated testing covered
entries.source: Deque, Automated testing study identifies 57 percent of digital accessibility issues (2021-03-10)
entries.quote: Deque found that, on average, 57 percent of accessibility issues were completely covered by this automated testing.

entries.claim: the size of Deque's data set
entries.quote: over 2,000 audits in various industries, spanning over 13,000 pages (all first-time page assessments) covering nearly 300,000 issues

entries.claim: home pages with detected WCAG 2 failures, and detected errors per page
entries.source: WebAIM Million (2026)
entries.quote: 95.9% of home pages had detected WCAG 2 failures ... 56.1 errors per page

entries.claim: home pages with each of the six most common failures: low-contrast text, missing alt text, missing form labels, empty links, empty buttons, missing document language
entries.source: WebAIM Million (2026)
entries.quote: Low contrast text 83.9%; Missing alternative text for images 53.1%; Missing form input labels 51.0%; Empty links 46.3%; Empty buttons 30.6%; Missing document language 13.5%

entries.claim: screen reader and browser pairings: NVDA with Chrome 21.3%, JAWS with Chrome 24.7%, NVDA with Firefox 10.0%
entries.source: WebAIM Screen Reader User Survey #10 (December 2023 to January 2024)
entries.quote: JAWS with Chrome 24.7%; NVDA with Chrome 21.3%; NVDA with Firefox 10.0%

entries.claim: the size of the 2018 eye-tracking study
entries.source: Nielsen Norman Group, Scrolling and Attention (2018)
entries.quote: 120 participants ... over 130,000 fixations

entries.claim: viewing time above the fold (2018), in the first two screenfuls (2018), and above the fold in the 2010 study
entries.source: Nielsen Norman Group, Scrolling and Attention (2018)
entries.quote: 57% of their page-viewing time above the fold ... 74% of the viewing time was spent in the first two screenfuls ... 80% of the viewing time was made up of fixations above the fold

entries.claim: the average documented cart-abandonment rate, across 50 studies
entries.source: Baymard Institute, Cart abandonment rate statistics
entries.quote: 70.22% – average documented online shopping cart abandonment rate (based on 50 different studies)

entries.claim: form fields in the average US checkout, form elements in it, and the ideal number of fields
entries.source: Baymard Institute, Cart abandonment rate statistics
entries.quote: an ideal checkout flow can be as short as 12-14 form elements (7-8 if only counting the form fields) ... the average US checkout flow contains 23.48 form elements displayed to users by default. (14.88 if only counting the form fields.)

entries.claim: the retail conversion lift associated with a 0.1 s mobile speed improvement, observational, 37 sites and 30M+ sessions at the end of 2019
entries.source: Deloitte and Google, Milliseconds Make Millions (web.dev case study)
entries.quote: The research team studied 37 leading European and American brand sites, collecting data on over 30 million user sessions. ... retail sites seeing an increase of 8.4% in conversion rates

entries.claim: the population threshold for the earlier ADA Title II compliance date
entries.source: U.S. Department of Justice, ADA Title II web rule (as extended in April 2026)
entries.quote: The compliance date for State and local government entities with a total population of 50,000 or more [is extended] to April 26, 2027.

entries.claim: when Supabase stops supporting the legacy anon and service_role API keys
entries.source: Supabase docs, Migrating to publishable and secret API keys
entries.quote: Supabase is deprecating the `anon` and `service_role` keys by the end of 2026.

entries.claim: the point past which Supabase recommends Broadcast over Postgres Changes
entries.source: Supabase docs, Realtime: Postgres Changes
entries.quote: If you expect more than ~3,000 concurrent subscribers on the same changes, use Broadcast to stream database changes

entries.claim: the largest ratio of a fluid size's maximum to its minimum that always passes WCAG SC 1.4.4 under browser zoom
entries.source: Maxwell Barvian, Addressing Accessibility Concerns With Using Fluid Type, Smashing Magazine, 7 November 2023
entries.quote: If the maximum font size is less than or equal to 2.5 times the minimum font size, then the text will always pass WCAG SC 1.4.4, at least on all modern browsers.

entries.claim: typescript-eslint's latest release, 8.71.0, accepts TypeScript below 6.1.0 (its peer range is >=4.8.4 <6.1.0)
entries.source: npm registry, typescript-eslint 8.71.0 (the version's manifest)

entries.claim: npm's latest TypeScript, the version an unpinned install gets
entries.source: npm registry, typescript's dist-tags

entries.claim: web.dev's good TTFB, which it calls a rough guide
entries.source: web.dev, Time to First Byte (TTFB)
entries.quote: As a rough guide, most sites should strive to have a TTFB of 0.8 seconds or less.

entries.claim: the Git LFS storage, and the LFS bandwidth a month, that GitHub Free includes; a workflow's LFS checkout spends the owner's bandwidth
entries.source: GitHub Docs, Git Large File Storage billing
entries.quote: The following amounts of storage and bandwidth for downloads are included in your GitHub plan. [Plan, Bandwidth, Storage] GitHub Free: 10 GiB, 10 GiB. [...] If GitHub Actions downloads a 500 MB file that is tracked with Git LFS, it will use 500 MB of the repository owner's bandwidth. [...] If you use more than your included quota of bandwidth per month without a payment method on file, Git LFS support is disabled on your account until the next month.

entries.claim: the repository size GitHub recommends
entries.source: GitHub Docs, About large files on GitHub
entries.quote: We recommend repositories remain small, ideally less than 1 GB, and less than 5 GB is strongly recommended.

entries.claim: the factor Lighthouse's DevTools throttling multiplies its 150 ms RTT by, as per-request latency, with 0.9 of the throughput: measure_vitals' `lighthouse` preset
entries.source: Chrome DevTools frontend, front_end/models/trace/lantern/simulation/Constants.ts (Lighthouse's throttling constants), commit 828ccd43
entries.quote: const DEVTOOLS_RTT_ADJUSTMENT_FACTOR = 3.75; const DEVTOOLS_THROUGHPUT_ADJUSTMENT_FACTOR = 0.9; [...] mobileSlow4G: { rttMs: 150, throughputKbps: 1.6 * 1024, requestLatencyMs: 150 * DEVTOOLS_RTT_ADJUSTMENT_FACTOR, downloadThroughputKbps: 1.6 * 1024 * DEVTOOLS_THROUGHPUT_ADJUSTMENT_FACTOR, uploadThroughputKbps: 750 * DEVTOOLS_THROUGHPUT_ADJUSTMENT_FACTOR, cpuSlowdownMultiplier: 4, }

entries.claim: the spam rate in Google's Postmaster Tools a sender should stay below, and the rate it should never reach
entries.source: Google Workspace Admin Help, Email sender guidelines
entries.quote: Keep spam rates reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.10% and avoid ever reaching a spam rate of 0.30% or higher.

entries.claim: how soon Google advises fulfilling an unsubscribe request
entries.source: Google Workspace Admin Help, Email sender guidelines FAQ
entries.quote: we recommend that you fulfill unsubscribe requests within 48 hours, a reasonable timeline for removing recipients from a mailing list.

entries.claim: the size of an email's HTML part past which Gmail clips it behind "View entire message", as the ESPs document it; Google publishes no figure, and the byte-exact 102,400 is from measurement, which the docs say
entries.source: Mailmodo, Why are my emails getting clipped in Gmail? (last updated 2025-11-04); DailyStory, HTML email clipping limits across different mailbox providers (updated 2026-03-17) says the same
entries.quote: If your HTML email is more than 102kb, then Gmail will clip your email.

entries.claim: the ceiling on <style> content in Gmail, raised from 8,192 bytes; every element that crosses it is removed with every one after it
entries.source: hteumeuleu/email-bugs, issue #90 "Gmail limits <style> to 16 kB" (opened 2021-03-02)
entries.quote: Gmail supports up to 8192 bytes of styles. (And this has been recently updated to 16384 bytes according to Eric Lepetit on the Emailgeeks Slack.)

entries.claim: the share of usability problems five users find in a qualitative study, when each user finds 31% (NN/g's five-user rule)
entries.source: Nielsen Norman Group, Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users (2000)
entries.quote: The typical value of L is 31%, averaged across a large number of projects we studied. ... After the first study with five participants has found 85% of the usability problems, you will want to fix these problems in a redesign.

entries.claim: how many users NN/g recommends for a quantitative usability study
entries.source: Nielsen Norman Group, Quantitative Studies: How Many Users to Test? (2006)
entries.quote: I usually recommend testing with 20 users when collecting quantitative usability metrics.

entries.claim: how many men have a color vision deficiency
entries.source: National Eye Institute, Color Blindness
entries.quote: About 1 in 12 men have color vision deficiency

not_statistics.why: an example of a claimed lift, quoted as one that does not replicate
the measured cut, qualified in the sentence as measurement; the registered figure is the ESPs' 102 KB
